post.description:
### Why this endpoint issues a challengeId

A provider telling us an email address is verified does not prove the caller owns the account already registered to
it. So when the Google or Apple email matches an existing verified account, this endpoint answers **409
`ACCOUNT_LINK_REQUIRED`** rather than signing anyone in, emails a code to that address, and returns a `challengeId`
(one use, 10 minutes). Finish at `POST /auth/oauth/link`.

A new email address signs up here and returns tokens straight away — the 409 only happens when there is an account
to protect.

### Finishing an account link

Send the `challengeId` from the 409 `ACCOUNT_LINK_REQUIRED` answer, together with the code emailed to the existing
account:

```json
{ "challengeId": "<from the 409>", "code": "123456" }
```

The provider identity is attached to that account and the caller signs in; from then on either the password or the
provider gets them in. A wrong, expired or already-used code, and an unknown challenge, all answer the same 401, so
start again from the provider sign-in.

### The onboarding gate

`profileCompletedAt` stays null until first name, last name, date of birth and gender are all present. Email sign-ups
send the name and date of birth at sign-up; Google and Apple sign-ups may arrive with nothing. Gender is never asked
at sign-up, so every new account starts with a null `profileCompletedAt`, which is the cue to show the onboarding
screen. `isNew: true` on the sign-in answer says it is the first sign-in.

`PATCH /me` sets the stamp itself the moment all four are filled in. There is no separate "finish onboarding" call.

post.description:
### Setting a profile picture

One call. Send the image as `multipart/form-data` under the field name `file` and the answer carries the URL the
picture is served from. There is no upload ticket to fetch first and nothing to poll afterwards.

1. Pick the photo on the device and resize it before sending. A phone camera easily produces 10 MB; the limit here is 5 MB.
2. `POST /me/avatar` with the bytes as `file`. JPEG, PNG and WebP are accepted, decided by reading the file rather than
   by what the request claims it is.
3. Show `avatarUrl` from the answer. It is a public, cacheable URL and needs no token to load.

The image is re-encoded server-side into a 200 px square for lists and an 800 px version for the full profile;
`avatarUrl` points at the small one, and location data in the original is dropped. A new picture gets a new URL, so a
cached old one never shows in its place. `DELETE /me/avatar` clears it again.

post.description:
### The gallery

Up to six photos, on top of the profile picture. Same upload as the avatar: send the image as `multipart/form-data`
under the field name `file` and the answer carries the URLs it is served from.

1. `POST /me/photos` with the bytes as `file`. The seventh one is a 409, so show the count.
2. Each photo comes back with `url` (1280 px, for the full-screen view), `thumbUrl` (400 px, for the grid) and its
   `position` in the gallery.
3. `PUT /me/photos/order` with every photo id in the order you want them. Send the whole list, not the part that moved.
4. `DELETE /me/photos/{photoId}` takes one out and closes the gap; the files are deleted a moment later.

The avatar is separate and unchanged: it is the small square shown in lists and chat, and it has its own endpoints.

### Trips

A trip is a city and the dates you are there. While one covers today, your profile reads as visiting that city
instead of only as a local of your home city.

- Up to five trips that have not ended yet. A past trip is kept but does not count and is not listed here.
- At most 90 days each, and at most a year ahead.
- Two trips may not cover the same day, but leaving one city and arriving in the next on the same date is fine.

Other people see only the city you are in today. The dates, and any trip that has not started, are yours alone.

post.description:
### Getting a verified badge

A person sends one selfie. A moderator opens it beside their profile picture and decides whether it is the
same face. There is no document to upload and no third party involved.

1. Make sure the account has a profile picture. Without one there is nothing to compare against, so the
   selfie is refused with a 409 rather than queued.
2. `POST /me/verification` with the image as `multipart/form-data` under the field name `file`. JPEG, PNG and
   WebP are accepted, decided by reading the bytes rather than by what the request claims.
3. Poll `GET /me/verification`, or wait for the email. `status` moves from `pending` to `approved` or
   `rejected`.

Only one request can be open at a time. After a rejection the next selfie is accepted 24 hours later, and
`canReapplyAt` on the status answer says exactly when; asking sooner returns `VERIFICATION_COOLDOWN` with the
same moment in `details.retryAfter`.

The selfie is never shown publicly and is deleted within seven days of the decision. Changing the profile
picture afterwards does not remove the badge.

tags.description:
Sign-in here can take two calls, because the first credential is not always enough on its own. Rather than sign the
caller in, the server parks the half-finished attempt and hands back an id naming it. Send that id with the second
proof and the sign-in completes.

In the mobile app that id is a `challengeId`: a random uuid, not a token. It carries no signature, unlocks nothing on
its own, and is useless without the code that goes with it. Every challenge lasts 10 minutes and works once — spending
it, letting it expire, or running out of attempts all discard it, and the caller starts again from the first call.
Admin sign-in is two-step too, but names its half-finished attempt with a pending token.
